nameStory: The Trogulid Harvestman gets its name from the Greek word 'troglos,' meaning cave or hole, referring to its secretive habits of hiding in leaf litter and debris. These arachnids are part of the harvestman family, earning that common name because they're most often noticed during harvest time in late summer and fall when they emerge from their hiding spots.
description: The Trogulid Harvestman is a small, flattened arachnid that looks quite different from typical daddy longlegs. Growing only 7-9mm long, it has a distinctly pancake-flat body and unusually short, sturdy legs compared to other harvestmen. Young specimens start out violet-colored before maturing to brown, and they're almost always covered in bits of dirt and debris that stick to their body.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly flattened and narrow body, like a tiny oval pancake, completely unlike the round bodies of most harvestmen

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small at 7-9mm body length with legs reaching only about 8mm - you could easily fit several on a dime

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves extremely slowly and deliberately, often appearing motionless, and is typically covered in particles of dirt that stick to its surface

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Young individuals are violet-colored while adults are brownish, often with three ridges (carinae) running along the back that you can feel with gentle touch

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Unusually short and robust legs for a harvestman, feeling sturdy rather than delicate when gently handled

habitat: Look for Trogulid Harvestmen in areas with limestone or other calcium-rich soils, particularly in leaf litter under deciduous trees. They prefer moist, sheltered spots where snails are common, such as the base of stone walls, under logs, or in compost-rich forest floor debris.

seasonality.spring: Adults are active but well-hidden in leaf litter. Young violet-colored specimens may be found molting as they grow toward maturity.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are hunting snails and other small prey. Look for them in the evening when they're most mobile.
seasonality.fall: Easiest time to spot them as they prepare for winter, often found under logs and in deep leaf litter accumulations.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in leaf litter or under protective debris, remaining inactive until warmer weather returns.

funFact: This tiny harvestman is actually a snail specialist that uses empty snail shells as nurseries - after eating the snail, the female lays her eggs right inside the shell, turning her victim's home into a perfect baby cradle!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small spiders due to its compact size, but remember that harvestmen have their body in one piece (no waist) and don't make webs. The flattened shape immediately distinguishes it from all other harvestmen in New England.
contextualKnowledge: This species is actually a European introduction to North America, representing one of the less common cases of Old World arachnids successfully establishing in New England. Despite being called harvestmen like daddy longlegs, these belong to a completely different family with very different habits.
compareHints: As the only Trogulus species in our region, compare it with Anelasmocephalus cambridgei, which is smaller and less flattened. The Trogulid's distinctly pancake-flat body and dirt-covered appearance make it unique among New England harvestmen - no other species in the region has such a compressed, debris-laden appearance.
